history.heading: Colonial history
paragraphs: Trinidad and Tobago, two islands off the coast of Venezuela, were inhabited by Arawak and Carib peoples. Columbus named Trinidad in 1498. Spain held Trinidad but settled it sparsely until the 1780s, when it invited French Catholic planters and their enslaved Africans. Britain captured Trinidad in 1797; Tobago changed hands many times before becoming British in 1814.

After slavery was abolished in 1834, about 150,000 indentured labourers were brought from India between 1845 and 1917, along with Chinese and Portuguese workers. The islands were united as one colony in 1889.

history.heading: Oil and independence
paragraphs: Oil was discovered in the early 20th century, and labour unrest in 1937 led to the rise of trade unions. Trinidad and Tobago became independent on 31 August 1962 under historian Eric Williams and became a republic in 1976. An attempted coup by the Jamaat al Muslimeen in 1990 failed.

culture.heading: Carnival and music
paragraphs: Trinidad and Tobago is the birthplace of calypso, soca, limbo and the steelpan, the only acoustic instrument invented in the 20th century. Carnival, before Lent, is one of the world's greatest, with masquerade bands and steelband competitions (Panorama).

The population is mainly of Indian and African descent, with mixed and other communities. English is official. Christianity, Hinduism and Islam are all major religions; Diwali and Eid are public holidays. Doubles, roti and pelau are popular dishes. Writer V. S. Naipaul won the Nobel Prize in Literature, and cricketer Brian Lara is a legend.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Trinidad and Tobago is a parliamentary republic. Politics has been dominated by the People's National Movement, mainly supported by Afro-Trinidadians, and the United National Congress, mainly supported by Indo-Trinidadians. The UNC won the 2025 election. Tobago has its own House of Assembly. Violent crime is a major concern.

economy.heading: Energy economy
paragraphs: Trinidad and Tobago is one of the wealthiest countries in the Caribbean, thanks to oil and especially natural gas. It is a major exporter of liquefied natural gas, ammonia and methanol. Declining gas production is a challenge, and the country is seeking new supplies, including from Venezuela. The currency is the Trinidad and Tobago dollar.
